pl-l4d23c2-d1e112.summary: Describes the first anointing, with chrism, called principal because the Paraclete is principally given in it; for abundance of grace it has two liquids mixed, oil and the balsam of good repute. 'Chrisma' is Greek for anointing; not all holy oil is called chrism, only that mixed with balsam, with which the heads of kings and bishops are anointed, the priest anoints the baptized on the crown, and the bishop anoints the confirmed on the forehead.
claims: Chrism is oil mixed with balsam, the principal anointing.
Chrism is used for kings, bishops, baptism, and confirmation.

pl-l4d23c2-d1e118.summary: Describes another anointing, with which catechumens and neophytes are anointed on the breast and between the shoulders at baptism.
claims: Catechumens are anointed on breast and shoulders.

pl-l4d23c2-d1e124.summary: Describes the third, the oil of the sick, which is now treated.

pl-l4d23c2-d1e130.summary: A heading encoded as a paragraph: 'By whom this sacrament was instituted'.

pl-l4d23c2-d1e134.summary: States that this sacrament of the anointing of the sick is read to have been instituted by the apostles.
claims: The anointing of the sick was instituted by the apostles.

pl-l4d23c2-d1e140.summary: Cites James: is any sick among you? let him bring in the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the Lord's name, and the Lord will relieve him, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven. So the sacrament was instituted for two reasons, remission of sins and relief of bodily illness; whoever receives it faithfully and devoutly is relieved in body and soul, if relief of both is expedient; if bodily health is not expedient, he gains health of soul.
claims: The anointing remits sins and relieves bodily illness.
Bodily healing is given when expedient; spiritual health always.

pl-l4d23c2-d1e155.summary: States that as in other sacraments, here too the sacrament is one thing and its reality another: the sacrament is the outward anointing; the reality the inward anointing, perfected by remission of sins and increase of virtues. Omitting this sacrament through contempt or negligence is dangerous and damnable.
claims: The sacrament is outward anointing; its reality inward anointing.
Neglecting it through contempt is damnable.

pl-l4d23c2.summary: Distinguishes three anointings: chrism, the principal anointing, in which the Paraclete is principally given, mixing oil and balsam, used for kings and bishops, for the crown of the baptized, and for the forehead of the confirmed; the oil of catechumens, anointing breast and shoulders at baptism; and the oil of the sick. Under a heading on its institution, it was instituted by the apostles, as James shows: the elders pray and anoint the sick, the Lord relieves him, and sins are forgiven. It is for remission of sins and relief of bodily illness, giving bodily health when expedient and always health of soul. Its sacrament is the outward anointing, its reality the inward anointing perfected by remission of sins and increase of virtues; omitting it through contempt or negligence is dangerous and damnable.
claims: There are three anointings: chrism, oil of catechumens, oil of the sick.
Chrism, of oil and balsam, is the principal anointing.
The anointing of the sick was instituted by the apostles, as James shows.
It remits sins and relieves bodily illness when expedient.
Its reality is inward anointing: remission of sins and increase of virtues.
Neglecting it through contempt is damnable.
